author: mahmutefedara
body:
The two findings #29's final review turned up and deliberately left open. Both are the same shape as things that PR already fixed — which is the point: its closing note said the general form was worth one deliberate sweep, and these are what the sweep found.

## A card stays on its board

`0028` closed two `ideas` findings and missed a third column. It pinned `workspace_id` with a `WITH CHECK` and froze `created_by` with a trigger, but `ideas.session_id` is pinned by nothing — and PostgREST is reachable with the anon key that ships in the browser bundle, so `PATCH /rest/v1/ideas?id=eq.<mine>` moves a card onto a different brainstorm board.

`0028`'s own `WITH CHECK` does not stop it, and the reason is worth stating because it is easy to misread as covered: the check compares `workspace_id` against *the parent session's*. After the move the new session **is** the parent, so it is satisfied against the very row that just changed.

The effect is a `viewer` — whose contract in `src/lib/roles.ts` is "Uses the agents. Changes none of them." — putting a card on a shared board they are only supposed to read. It is contained: the subquery runs under the caller's own RLS, so a non-member gets `NULL` and fails. Nothing crosses a tenant boundary.

`0030` adds a `before update` trigger holding `session_id` immutable, in the same shape as the two `0028` already carries. A separate function rather than widening `0028`'s, because the two invariants are unrelated and each deserves its own error message. The route agrees with the database now: `updateIdeaSchema` has never had a `session_id` field, so nothing legitimate wanted to change it — the same argument `0027` made for a routine's `source_config`.

## The whole stack, not just covan-api

#29 made `covan-api` refuse to boot on the credentials `.env.docker.example` ships when `ALLOWED_ORIGIN` is not localhost. That left a real gap, and `docs/self-hosting.md` said so plainly rather than implying otherwise: `JWT_SECRET` and `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` are consumed by Kong, GoTrue, PostgREST and Postgres, none of which run `loadEnv`. So an operator who sets `BIND_ADDR=0.0.0.0` without regenerating those two still exposes a superuser Postgres and a Kong whose JWTs anyone can forge, while `covan-api` crash-loops beside them. Those values are in this repository; the demo JWTs verify against the shipped secret and are valid until 2027-01-09.

The fix is a `secrets-check` init container, not a guard in `docker/kong-entrypoint.sh`. Kong is the wrong choke point — it leaves Postgres on `54322` open. Every service here descends from `db`:

```
auth <- db      rest <- db      realtime <- db
kong <- auth rest               migrate <- db auth
covan-api <- migrate kong       covan-web <- covan-api
```

so one container that `db` waits on gates the entire stack. It also has to be this direction: making `db` depend on `covan-api` is circular, since `covan-api -> kong -> auth -> db`.

`docker/check-secrets.sh` mirrors `loadEnv`'s shape deliberately, so the two cannot drift into disagreeing. Localhost-only `ALLOWED_ORIGIN` allows everything — that is a laptop, and the demo values are what it is for — with the same every-entry semantics `env.ts` uses, so one non-local origin in a comma-separated list defeats the exemption. Otherwise it refuses on `JWT_SECRET`, `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`, `SECRET_KEY_BASE`, `ANON_KEY`, `SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` or `ROUTINE_SECRET_KEY`, naming every offender in one message rather than making an operator fix them one restart at a time. It does not re-check `ROUTINE_SECRET_KEY`'s decoded length — `loadEnv` already owns that, and a second copy in shell would only be a worse one.

It runs on `postgres:17.6-alpine`, which `migrate` already pulls, so a fresh `docker compose up` downloads nothing new.

`docs/self-hosting.md`'s "What it cannot enforce is the rest of step 1" paragraph is now wrong, so it is replaced rather than left standing next to a contradiction.

## Verifying this

**The RLS job is the gate for `0030`.** The Docker daemon on the machine this was written on went unhealthy partway through — zero containers, hanging on `docker info` — so the RLS suite could not run locally and the `secrets-check` script could not be exercised inside its real BusyBox image. The script's logic was verified instead by running it directly under `sh` and `dash` with hand-set environments, including the two adversarial cases worth naming: `ALLOWED_ORIGIN="http://localhost:3000,https://evil.com"` must refuse, and `http://localhost.evil.com` must not count as local. Both behave correctly.

The six literals were compared byte-for-byte against `.env.docker.example` rather than by eye — a single character of drift would make the guard silently never fire, which is the failure mode that matters most here.

Unit tests, typechecks and lint are green locally (261 frontend, 483 worker, 0 lint errors).

## Two cosmetic notes, deliberately not fixed

`check-secrets.sh`'s `localhost_only()` uses `set --` to word-split the origin list, which permanently overwrites the script's own positional parameters. It cannot bite today — compose invokes the script with no arguments and nothing after that call reads `$@` — but it is a trap if anyone later adds argument handling. And the file carries a `755` bit that goes unused, since compose runs it as `/bin/sh /check-secrets.sh`.

## After merging

`0030` needs applying by hand alongside `0026`–`0029`. CI does not apply migrations. Confirm the project ref first — a retired Supabase project stays reachable and answers exactly like the live one.

author: ahliweb
body:
`skills:check` exists on the premise that a wrong skill is worse than a stale doc,
because an agent **follows** a skill. Its rule 1 read `src/…` citations and
nothing else — so `tests/`, `scripts/`, `openapi/`, `deploy/`, `ops/` and `docs/`
were ungoverned. That is exactly where a skill does its most operational talking:
which test proves a claim, which script to run, which runbook to follow before a
production migration.

A sweep found ~60 citations that resolve to nothing. They did not fail
cosmetically.

### `awcms-production-preflight` told an operator to break the backup

Its banner correctly says `bun run production:preflight` does not exist. Forty
lines below, a section described `scripts/production-preflight.ts` in detail —
ten stages, three mandatory apply flags, an `authorizeApply` "covered by unit
tests". None of it has ever been in this repo.

Worse: §Backup & restore told the operator to set `BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY_FILE` /
`BACKUP_HMAC_KEY_FILE` before the go-live backup. `deploy/backup/backup-postgres.sh`
**refuses to run** when either is set — its own `die()` says at-rest encryption
and manifest signing are not implemented. Following the skill literally broke the
last step before a production migration.

### `awcms-profile-identity` denied a whole test tier

It stated twice that this repo has no `tests/integration/` "at all yet (Issue
#154)". #154 landed: a harness and ~74 specs. An agent following that skill skips
the tier entirely.

### Rule 6

Same shape as rule 1, over the other governed directories, across both language
copies of every skill and every module README. Three deliberate carve-outs, each
because the first draft got it wrong against the real corpus:

- **`sql/` is not governed** — `sql/005` is a migration *number*, not a path;
  `check:docs` already validates those by number.
- **An absence claim is exempt** — "there is no `deploy/backup/README.md`" must
  stay sayable, or the gate deletes the sentences that correct the record.
  Required at *every* occurrence, so one honest paragraph cannot license a second
  live-sounding one.
- **Sibling-repo citations are scoped, not banned** — `awcms-mini:tests/…` names a
  file this repo cannot check; an unprefixed path is a claim about THIS repo.

Mutation-proven against the real sentences: each defect goes red, and absence
claims, sibling-repo citations, globs and resolving paths stay green.

### Rebase note

Rebased onto `main` after v10.0.0. The only conflict was the
`i18n-source-hash` marker in `docs/PROJECT_STATE.id.md` — recomputed with
`docs:i18n:stamp` rather than resolved by picking a side, since neither
pre-rebase value describes the merged English source.

### Verification

All 52 gates + typecheck + astro checks + build green; suite **5938 pass**. The
single failure is `the committed bundle > matches its TypeScript source`, a
local-only artefact of Bun 1.4.0 vs CI's pinned 1.3.14 (minifier identifier
naming); the bundle was deliberately not regenerated.

author: shoto290
body:
The runtime registry landed in #367: one conversation controller per room, held above the screens, shut down only when the app closes. Nothing ever dropped one, so a deleted room kept a live controller subscribed for the rest of the session.

## What changed

- `conversation-runtimes.ts` — `release(conversationId)` deletes the entry from the map first, then awaits `runtime.shutdown()` behind a `.catch`, so a refusing runtime is forgotten anyway. No-op on an unknown id.
- `App.tsx` — `deleteConversation(id)` mirrors the existing `deleteBot` pattern: release, then remove from the store. Both delete sites — the sidebar menu and the settings dialog — go through it.
- `conversation-runtimes.test.ts` — one test per contract clause.

## Notes

- Released before removing from the store: the reverse order lets a live turn write into a conversation that no longer exists.
- `ConversationController.shutdown()` only calls `driver.shutdown` when a turn is live; with no active speaker it just disconnects. Left as is — changing it would move app-close behavior too. The "stop the answer" test therefore releases mid-turn.
- The local `started`/`wrote` fixtures derive a message id from the bot id alone, so one bot answering twice in a room collides. The reopen tests use the exported `spoke` helper, which ids by text length.

No idle timeout or any other eviction rule beyond deletion. No changes to `roster-controller.ts` or `roster-conversations.ts`. No markup, so no design-system surface.

## Verify

`bun run types` clean · `bun run lint` clean · `bun run test:unit` 847/847

**🎯 要回复（购买意向）** - 询价：多少钱、**多少、啥价**、怎么卖、包邮、优惠、how much、price - 产品问题：尺码、颜色、材质、有货、**有m吗**、链接、**第几张、图几、怎么拿、po一下**、size、color、in stock - 购买意向：想买、下单、求链接、有链接吗、**主页**、want to buy - **🚫 广告/导流（建议删除）** - 站外引流：微信、vx、威信、薇信、check my bio、dm me、telegram - author: gradkh
body:
Rebased and taken over from an unpushed local branch (`perf/match-python-parallelism`, `b1b0944` + `46b2d84`) that was at risk of being lost with its worktree. Original authorship and commit messages preserved; the only change I made was resolving one conflict.

## What it does

The nightly War and Peace benchmark (one 3.2 MB document, 171 chunks in both SDKs) measured cognify p50 at **306s for Python vs 802–867s for Rust**. The same Rust run with `LLM_MAX_PARALLEL_REQUESTS=200` took **265s** — so the whole gap was queueing discipline in front of the same API, not work done.

Rust drained extraction as `chunks_per_batch=100` slices with a hard `join_all` barrier between them, capping in-flight calls inside a slice at `max_parallel_extractions=20` — nine serialised waves for 171 chunks, with the LLM idle behind the slowest call in each.

This replaces the batched `join_all` with `futures::stream::iter(..).map(..).buffered(max_parallel)`, so a freed slot refills immediately instead of waiting for the wave. `buffered` rather than `buffer_unordered` because `all_graphs` order feeds order-sensitive dedup in `retrieve_existing_edges`. Because `buffered` only polls up to `max_parallel` futures, per-chunk text clones are created lazily rather than all up front — a small memory win over the old code.

Summarisation needed no restructuring; it already streams unbatched through `buffer_unordered` with a re-sort.

## Python parity, verified empirically

Checked against the real Python pipeline with a fake LLM client, not read off the source:

- The extraction task carries `task_config` `batch_size=2000` — `cognify.py:60` defaults the argument to `None`, `cognify.py:367` falls back to a 2000 literal because `modules/cognify/config.py:12` is also `None`, and `cognify.py:388` attaches it. Driving 171 chunks through the real `run_tasks_base` yields **exactly one invocation of 171 chunks**, so there is no barrier at this document size.
- Concurrency inside that batch is **unbounded**. Measured max in-flight was 171 for extraction (`extract_graph_from_data.py:191`) and 171 for summarisation (`summarize_text.py:58`), with no semaphore and `llm_rate_limit_enabled` `False` by default (`infrastructure/llm/config.py:151`).

Hence `PYTHON_CHUNKS_PER_BATCH = 2000`, with `chunks_per_batch` and `max_parallel_extractions` both defaulting to it so the cap is non-binding — identical to Python's gather — while remaining a real, reachable ceiling (`LLM_MAX_PARALLEL_REQUESTS=1` stays the documented way to serialise for replay cassettes).

## Rebase note

One conflict, in `crates/lib/src/config.rs`. `main` gained `llm_min_retry_seconds: 240` from #144 after this branch was written; kept both that and the branch's `llm_max_parallel_requests` change. Chunking is untouched, so replay cassettes stay valid.

## ⚠️ Open question for review — the default concurrency, given #144

**This branch predates #144**, and I think that changes the calculus on the *number*, not the mechanism.

#144 added an overload policy: on a 429/503/529 or a timeout, a token bucket engages at `llm_rate_limit_requests=60` / `llm_rate_limit_interval=60` — **1 req/s — for a 900s cooldown**. Bursting 2000 concurrent requests at a rate-limited endpoint is close to a guaranteed way to open that episode, after which the run crawls for 15 minutes. At 650k chunks that is ~325 batches, so ~325 opportunities to trip it.

Two further points against 2000 specifically:

- **The measurement supports ~200, not 2000.** The 265s figure came from `LLM_MAX_PARALLEL_REQUESTS=200`. Nothing measured 2000.
- **`70c58dd` observed the provider degrading under load** — per-call latency rose 76s → 97s going from 20 to 100 in flight. Extrapolating to 2000 is unsupported.

The counter-argument is real and may win: **Python has the same combination** — unbounded gather *and* the 900s cooldown, which #144 ported from it — so 2000 is the faithful parity choice, and parity is the project's stated tiebreaker.

I have deliberately **not** changed the authored value. The barrier removal is the unambiguous win and is what the measurement actually attributes the gain to; the 128 → 2000 cap raise is a separable, riskier change. Reviewer's call whether to ship 2000, or land the barrier fix with a measured cap (200, or the current 128) and revisit.

**This is the one open decision in the PR.** Everything else here is either the measured barrier fix or a rename; the default concurrency value is the part that wants a human call before merge.

## Verification

`cargo fmt --check`, `cargo check --all-targets`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` all clean. `cognee-cognify` 269 passed / 5 ignored across 30 suites.

author: yemfan
body:
The sender selected `sphere_contacts!inner`. `message_drafts.contact_id` was repointed to `contacts` by a later migration and this join was left behind.

An INNER join that matches nothing returns nothing — **no error, no warning, a 200 and an empty page**. The cron has been running green every fifteen minutes while dispatching none of it.

## Proven against production, before and after

```
select=…,sphere_contacts!inner(…)&status=eq.approved  →  0 rows
select=…,contacts!inner(…)&status=eq.approved         →  1 row
```

That one draft has been `approved` since **2 July**. Its `contact_id` resolves in `contacts` and not in `sphere_contacts`, which is the whole bug in one row.

Every column the sender reads — `phone`, `email`, `do_not_contact_sms`, `do_not_contact_email`, `preferred_language` — exists on `contacts`, so the embed is the entire change.

## A staleness guard, which the repair made necessary

With the join broken, approved drafts have been accumulating unsent. Fixing it would fire that backlog at real people.

A message written for a moment that has passed shouldn't arrive as though written today — *"just checking in about Saturday's showing"* is worse than silence three weeks later. Past a week, an approved draft now fails with a reason rather than sending.

## Why it matters beyond this file

This is what stood between the agent pressing approve and anything happening. It also silently blocked the drafts Chris now writes for inactive leads in [#1378](https://github.com/yemfan/helmsmart/pull/1378) — that feature would have looked broken for a reason nowhere near its own code.

## Verification

`npx vitest run` — 1531 passed, 138 files. `tsc --noEmit` clean. Join verified live in both directions.

author: shazron
body:
Closes [#148](https://github.com/shaztechio/bunyi-app/issues/148). History listed the same speaker twice:

```
Testing the mode switch unload.   PRESET VOICE  Ryan · Aug 24
Testing the mode switch unload.   PRESET VOICE  ryan · Aug 23
Once upon a time…                 PRESET VOICE  Serena · Aug 11
Once upon a time…                 PRESET VOICE  serena · Aug 11
```

## The fix is the .NET app's, not a new one

My first instinct was to lowercase the macOS fallback list so the value never changes. Checking the other app first is what stopped that:

- `apps/dotnet/tests/Core.Tests/DisplayNameTests.cs:26` describes **this exact bug** — *"the speaker list changed from `Ryan` to `ryan` the moment a model loaded"*.
- `OutputMetadata.VoiceSummary()` fixes it by normalising **when the value is read for a person**, with the comment: *"A clip made with `ryan` and one made with `Ryan` are the same voice and should not read as two."*

Two reasons that is the better fix, and both are why this PR follows it:

1. It repairs the **84 clips already on disk**. Changing the fallback list only fixes clips made from now on; the ones in the screenshot above would still read as two voices forever.
2. It keeps the apps solving one problem one way. A macOS-only fix here would be a divergence invented in ignorance of a solution the repo already had.

`DisplayName.of` mirrors `DisplayName.For` rule for rule — including that a single-letter word is uppercased whole while a longer word keeps its tail, so a name the model spelled deliberately is not rewritten.

`ContentView.speakerLabel` was the same function under another name, and is gone.

## Verified

The eleven cases `DisplayNameTests` pins, run in isolation: both spellings of `ryan`, `uncle_fu`, `ono_anna` and `serena`, plus empty, whitespace-only and single-character inputs. All match.

## Not verified, and I would like a second pair of eyes

**I could not confirm it on screen.** Accessibility permission was revoked partway through this work, so I could not bring the window forward to look at History. The change is a pure function applied at one call site and the build is clean, but the thing this issue is *about* is what the list looks like — so it is worth opening History and checking that every row now reads `Ryan`.

author: bechsteindigital
body:
Completes the useful half of #345. #360 let a plugin *declare* its keys; until they appear where an operator grants permissions, the plugin is still installed and still answering `403` — the declaration only moved the dead end into the manifest.

## A correction to #345

The issue said nothing could supply a permission key. That was **not quite right**, and the imprecision matters because it hides where the gap actually was.

`BackendPermissionInventory.All` already collected keys from `IHostAdminApiExtensionContributor.PermissionKeys`. A plugin contributing Admin-API routes could always supply its own.

What had no path was a plugin whose surface is `[CalloraRoute]` controllers — exactly the shape a marketplace plugin takes. Its routes demanded keys, and nothing could offer them.

Worth noting that this class of bug is on record here twice already. From the remark on `BackendPermissionKeyValidator`:

> Vorher verlangte diese Methode genau zwei Segmente aus einer festen Aktionsliste — und verschluckte damit jede Plugin-Berechtigung […] während die Endpunkte sie weiter verlangten. **Absicherung wirksam, Vergabe unmöglich.**

Same sentence, third occurrence.

## What changed

`BackendPermissionInventory.All` takes manifest-declared keys alongside contributed ones, and `GET /api/security/rbac/permissions` feeds both into one list. **Which supply path a plugin used is not something an operator should have to know.**

`PluginDeclaredPermissionCatalog` reads the manifests of installed plugins rather than keeping a table — the shape `ContractCatalogService` already uses. The manifest is the source of truth; a second copy is a second answer that can disagree, and the disagreement would surface as a key an operator can see but not grant. Uninstalled plugins drop out by construction, so there is no cleanup step to forget.

## Two deliberate choices

**Structurally invalid keys are filtered from the inventory**, even though manifest reading already refuses them. Not duplication: the inventory is also fed by installs whose manifest predates that check, and offering a key that can never match puts the operator back where they started.

**The catalog is a required dependency, not optional.** A silently missing service would mean silently missing keys — the original defect again, one layer up. One existing test had to register it rather than the parameter being made forgiving, which is the trade I want.

## Still open in #345

Route-level enforcement: a route requiring an *undeclared* key still fails at request time rather than being refused when the plugin activates. That needs the declarations available synchronously in `PluginApiEndpointDataSource.BuildEndpoints`, which is a different problem from this one and does not block the fix — with this merged, a plugin that declares correctly is fully usable.

## Verification

```

author: hankhsu1996
body:
## Summary

`$urandom` and `$urandom_range` (LRM 18.13.1 -- 18.13.2) now run on both backends, on the seeded generator model LRM 18.14 requires. The interesting part is not the draw, which any library supplies, but which generator a call draws from: the standard localizes randomness to threads and objects, so what this change really adds is the ownership and seeding of those generators.

## Two generators, and why they have opposite shapes

**A process generator** belongs to each process and serves every randomization call made from it (LRM 18.14.2). A process created by a `fork` starts from its creator's next value, so a whole subtree of threads follows from the seed of the one at its root, and the order those branches then run in moves none of it.

**An initialization generator** belongs to each module, interface, and program instance (LRM 18.14.1). It exists only because a static process has no creating thread to inherit from, and it hands seeds to the static processes and static initializers declared in that instance. The language can neither seed it nor read its state, and every instance's runs from the same default seed -- which is what keeps a change elsewhere in the design from moving what a given instance sees.

Annex P settles what counts as static here: every elaborated `initial`, `always`, `always_comb`, `always_latch`, `always_ff`, and continuous assignment.

## Registration names the instance to draw from

A process declared inside a generate scope belongs to the instance enclosing that scope, and both classes live in one artifact -- so the registration reaches that instance by typed navigation over a distance the lowering already knows, rather than by searching the object graph:

```cpp
Test::CreateProcesses()      -> RegisterInitialProcess(self, self, ...)
gen0_gen::CreateProcesses()  -> RegisterInitialProcess(self, static_cast<Test*>(self->Parent()), ...)
```

## What the corpus can and cannot check

Three cases under `18_random_value_generation`. Most of LRM 18.14 is about reproducibility across runs and robustness to unrelated edits, which one self-checking run cannot observe; what it can observe is asserted and nothing else:

| Case | What it holds the implementation to |
| --- | --- |
| `urandom_seed_reproduces_sequence` | the same seed replays the same draws |
| `urandom_range_bounds` | all three spellings of one range land in it; a range of one value is that value |
| `initialization_rng_is_per_instance` | two instances of one module draw alike |

The third is the one that discriminates: a single design-wide generator passes the first two and fails it. It reads LRM 18.14.1's "seeded with the default seed" literally, which is recorded as a deliberate reading rather than left implicit.

`$random` and the `$dist_*` family are deliberately not here. LRM 20.14 makes their algorithm normative and prints its C source in Annex N, so they carry their seed as an `inout` argument and touch none of the model above.

author: catradarusman
body:
The home surface was built for 11 pressed seconds and degrades badly on the way to 273. This reworks the parts that don't scale, and gives the piece an ending it can render.

All numbers below are measured in the browser, not estimated. Where something is arithmetic rather than a measurement, it says so.

## Rack

The press grid was one flat, unvirtualized list.

| | Before, at 273 | After |
|---|---|---|
| Page height, desktop | 14,314px (~20 screens) | constant, 12 pages of 24 |
| Page height, mobile | ~33,400px (~40 screens) | constant |
| Image payload | ~5.2MB | ~0.5MB |
| Grows with press count | yes | no |

Paginated at 24 (4 and 2 columns both divide it, so no page ends ragged). Added search by sleeve number, ENS name, or address, plus a **yours** filter when connected. Filtering is client-side over the existing read — paging through every page fires **0 new RPC calls**. Cards now seek the player to their second.

## ENS fan-out

`getEnsName` is one `eth_call` per holder. Sent one-per-holder on every 60s refetch, 273 holders is ~273 requests a minute against a free public node, which rate-limits and leaves every holder rendering as raw hex.

Batched through multicall and cached for the session:

| | Mainnet RPC calls |
|---|---|
| Before, per load (5 holders) | 5, all fired simultaneously |
| After, per load | 1 |
| Before, per 60s refetch | 5 more, forever |
| After, across 90s / 3 refetches | 0 more |

Verified CCIP-read still works through the batch by tracing `viem/actions/public/call.js`: `scheduleMulticall` sits inside the outer `try` whose `catch` handles the `OffchainLookup` revert.

Also fixed `staleTime` on the gallery query. At the default of 0, every additional observer refetched the whole gallery on mount — this caused a real regression during development (7 Base calls became 11+ in repeating clusters) which is fixed here.

## Complete state

`totalPressed === 273` had no branch anywhere. The site could reach its own ending and still read as in-progress.

| | Before at 273 | After |
|---|---|---|
| Progress caption | `273 of 273 seconds pressed` | `all 273 seconds pressed · 4′33″ is complete` |
| Rack header | `273 pressed · 0 silent` | `all 273 pressed` |
| CTA slot | `hold a sleeve? connect…` (dead) | `4′33″ is complete.` |
| About panel | `once all 273 are pressed…` forever | `all 273 are pressed…` |

The flag reads the contract's `totalPressed`, not the indexed array. Branch order is unsealed-sound → complete → everything else, so a holder who reserved a second but never saved audio keeps `finish saving your sound →`.

Note: the contract emits `AllSecondsPressed()` but has no airdrop function or flag, so the UI states the airdrop as process, not as something delivered. Showing delivered-vs-pending would need something onchain to read.

## Press journey

The CTA sat below the entire rack on mobile — 2.5 screens down at 11 pressed, 4.3 at a full page. Now 0.65 screens, directly under the player. Desktop placement is unchanged, pinned by grid column/row classes.

`/press` and `/press/[tokenId]` showed one line of grey text with no action when disconnected. Both now render a real connect button (verified it opens the ConnectKit modal).

Tagline widened 46ch → 56ch so it sets on one line on desktop (the string is 55 chars).

## Waveform

Marker thinning silently dropped whatever wouldn't fit — at 273 that's most of them. It now says `showing N of M presses`. Verified it reports fewer on narrower tracks (7 of 11 at 1280px, 5 of 11 at 375px).

## Testing

- `forge test` — **16 passed, 0 failed** across all three suites. No contract code changed in this PR.
- `tsc --noEmit` and `next build` clean.
- Every change verified live in the browser. Complete-state branches were tested by temporarily setting `TOTAL_SECONDS = 11` so they fired against real data; `constants.ts` is unmodified in this diff.

### Pre-merge gate status

Per `CLAUDE.md` §9, stating what ran and what did not rather than implying a full pass:

- **Suite green** — done, 16/16 above.
- **Security audit** — not run. This PR touches no contract code, no ownership, no audio storage, and adds no write paths; all new chain interaction is read-only. Worth a look before merge if you want it regardless.
- **Code review / testing-strategy skills** — not run. Flagging for the reviewer rather than skipping silently.

There is also a pre-existing `SyntaxError: Invalid or unexpected token` on localhost, next to a failed analytics fetch. Confirmed pre-existing by stashing this branch's changes and reproducing it. Unrelated, not addressed here.

body:
## What

Two leftovers in the sidebar are gone.

- A deleted room forgets its preview instead of keeping it for the rest of the session.
- A deleted bot leaves the avatar stack of every room it sat in, without a reload.
- A bot moved to another space empties the seats it held in the space it leaves.
- The last word of a deleted bot stays on the row, the name in front of it drops.
- A departed bot stays readable as the author of its own past messages.

## How

- `presentParticipants` now filters `leftAt === null && !isDeleted`, mirroring the seat rule the Rust side already applies.
- `removeConversation` drops the room's `conversationPreviews` entry, `remove` marks the bot's seats gone in the cached rooms, `moveToSpace` dismisses the bot from every room of the space it leaves before the move.
- The fake store keeps a deleted bot in a `departed` map so its seats still resolve with `isDeleted: true`, as the soft delete in SQLite does.

## Note

The move empties the seats for real (a persisted dismissal, `leftAt` set, lead re-crowned): `moved_bot` leaves the seats behind in SQLite, so a cache-only edit would come back on the next reload. Moving a bot back does not re-seat it, it has to be recruited again.

## Verified

`bun run types`, `bun run test:unit` (846 passing), `bun run lint`.

author: ameanasad
body:
## What problem does this change solve?

`tdx-measure verify` reported CCEL replay mismatches against **every** genuine TDREPORT. Two causes:

1. **Wrong register offsets.** `extract_rtmrs_from_tdreport()` read RTMR[0..3] at absolute offsets 720/768/816/864. Per the TDREPORT_STRUCT layout (Intel TDX Module spec), REPORTMACSTRUCT is 256 bytes and TDINFO's register block starts 328 bytes into TDINFO — the registers live at **584/632/680/728**. The code used `TDINFO_OFFSET=512` (+256) and windows 120 bytes short (exactly the five MRSEAM/MRSEAMSIGNER/attribute fields). The unit test encoded the same wrong offsets, so CI never caught it.
2. **RTMR[3] treated as a replay failure.** RTMR[3] is runtime-extendable and those extends never appear in the CCEL (the log covers firmware/boot events), so a replay mismatch there is *expected* on any guest that runtime-extends — e.g. confos extends the operator key into RTMR[3] from its initrd. With correct offsets, every real c8s guest still failed verify on exactly this register.

Validated against a live TDX quote from a production CVM: with the corrected offsets, replayed CCEL values match the hardware RTMR[0]/[1]/[2] (and equal the published build manifest values); RTMR[3] shows the operator-key value with an explanatory note.

## Why is this solution the best option to solve that problem?

- The offset is now **computed from the TDINFO field sizes** with the layout documented in a comment table — a silent repeat of the original mistake is structurally impossible.
- The unit test is rewritten as an **independent encoding of the spec** (literal spec offsets over a guard pattern): both original bug classes (wrong struct base, missing fields) now fail loudly instead of passing on zeros.
- The RTMR[3] verdict now matches attestation-rs's `verify_ccel_against_rtmrs` semantics (enforce RTMR[0..2]; RTMR[3] informational, "verify it against the quote directly"), keeping the two verification stacks consistent.
- Verification path only: measurement computation, build outputs, and measurements are untouched (noted in `CHANGELOG.md`).

## Checklist

- [x] `bin/test` passes (192 tests across 8 binaries, 5 skipped)
- [x] `bin/lint` is warning-free (rust 1.98.0, whole workspace)
- [x] `cargo deny check` passes (advisories/bans/licenses/sources ok; no `Cargo.toml`/`Cargo.lock` changes)
- [x] Commit messages follow [conventional commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/)
- [x] CLI flag changes are reflected in the README's matching table — **N/A**: no flag changes (behavior fix only; the command isn't in a README table)
- [x] Measurements of an unchanged config: **not altered** — verification path only; noted in `CHANGELOG.md`
- [x] Build pipeline determinism: **untouched** (no build-pipeline changes)
- [x] Kernel config snapshot: **N/A** (no kernel config change)
- [x] `kernel/version` bump: **N/A**

author: vjvarada
body:
**CP-11 slice 2.** The setting and the client that slice 3's serving hop needs.

**Ships DARK — nothing calls either.** `v1_compat.py` still serves
`/v1/chat/completions` from litellm directly. **H-41 stays open**, which is
correct: only slice 3 closes it.

## Where it lives, and why not a new module

`console_resolve.py`'s own header states it is THE Console httpx client. A
second one anywhere is root CLAUDE.md §5's defect by name. So the Router arm
lands beside the resolve, provision and seat arms. `_new_http_client` grew a
timeout **parameter** rather than a sibling factory. A test pins that the module
still builds exactly one `httpx.AsyncClient`.

## The credential is different, and that is the whole hazard

| Arm | Presents | For |
|---|---|---|
| resolve · provision · seat | `CUSTOMER_CONSOLE_DEPLOYMENT_KEY` (`cc_depl_`) | asking about PEOPLE |
| **Router (new)** | **`CUSTOMER_CONSOLE_ORG_KEY` (`cc_live_`)** | **spending AI CREDITS** |

`settings.py` already recorded why the names differ. It says this:

> *"Reusing one name for two credentials is how a box presents the wrong one
> and gets a 401 nobody can explain."*

Copying the seat arm and leaving its key read in place is the most likely way to
build this wrong. It would fail in production and not in CI. So it is asserted
and not assumed. `router_is_wired()` is separate from `is_wired()` for the same
reason. A box wired for sign-in is not thereby wired for AI.

## Three decisions worth your review

**No retry.** Every other arm tolerates one, because a resolve is idempotent. A
completion is not. The Console meters and CHARGES on the way through. A blind
retry of a request that actually succeeded bills the customer twice for one
answer.

**Its own timeout, 120s.** The 5s constant is tuned so an unreachable Console
degrades inside a person's patience at sign-in. Applied to a model call it would
abort essentially every real completion.

**501 is a VERDICT, not an outage.** The Router refuses streaming explicitly,
because CP-4b is unbuilt. 501 is a 5xx, so the outage rule every other arm uses
would swallow it. It would then report an unreachable Console. The caller's real
problem is that they asked for a stream.

**402 matters the same way.** "Out of credits", flattened into an outage, reads
as "the AI is down". That sends the customer to support instead of to the top-up
they actually need.

## Verification

28 tests, and **12 mutations killed, 0 survived**:

```
KILLED  M1  presents the DEPLOYMENT key instead of the org key
KILLED  M2  gates on is_wired() instead of router_is_wired()
KILLED  M3  router_is_wired accepts EITHER value (or, not and)
KILLED  M4  the 501 streaming carve-out is dropped
KILLED  M5  uses the SIGN-IN timeout for a completion
KILLED  M6  sends empty attribution headers instead of omitting them
KILLED  M7  402 out-of-credits is flattened into an outage
KILLED  M8  a retry loop is added 'for reliability'
KILLED  M9  the payload's model is coerced to a default tier
KILLED  M10 the trailing slash is not stripped from the URL
KILLED  M11 a non-dict body is passed through instead of normalised
KILLED  M12 the org-key setting is dropped from Settings
```

The tests were written after the code, so mutation testing is the honest proof
they bite. This path charges money, which is where this repo already asks for it.

⚠️ **The R8 suites around `console_resolve` SKIP on my machine** — they need a
real Postgres, and CI supplies it. 86 passed and 139 skipped locally. My own
suite needs no database and never skips.

## Two things slice 3 hits that nothing else did

Both are recorded on H-41 as well, so they are not carried by memory:

1. **`test_console_dependency_boundary.py` allows exactly FOUR importers of
   `console_resolve`, by equality.** `v1_compat.py` is a fifth. Widening
   `_ALLOWED_CALLERS` needs the argument written beside the name — the list's
   own rule. Slice 2 adds no importer, so the fence is untouched here.
2. **The 501.** Slice 3 must fall back or refuse explicitly. It must never
   de-stream in silence (§6B.5 hazard 1).

## Not done here

`CUSTOMER_CONSOLE_ORG_KEY` is not documented in any box template. The tenant
env template lives under `deploy/`, which is OWNER-GATE, and the root
`.env.example` carries no `CUSTOMER_CONSOLE_*` entry to sit beside.

⚠️ **On a SHARED multi-tenant box one org key cannot be right for every
tenant** — `seats.py` and `console_resolve.py:734` both already record this.
The setting is correct on a single-org silo. Slice 3 must resolve the key
per-organization before the flag can go on anywhere else. That is written in
the setting's own comment.

author: tomodo1773
body:
## 何を直したか

`arxiv.org/abs/{id}` は論文の入口で、**本文を1文字も含みません**。これまではそこをFirecrawlで取っていたため、保存されるのはアブストラクトだけでした。arXivがLaTeXMLで生成している全文HTMLから取るようにします。

実際の論文（[2608.18300](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.18300)）で、全9章と参考文献を含む48,342文字が保存されるようになりました。

## 取得はabsページを起点にする

absページには整ったメタデータ（`citation_*`）と、全文HTMLへの**版まで確定したリンク**の両方があります。ここを起点にすることで、

- 在庫の有無を404で確かめる必要がない（リンクの有無がarXiv自身の宣言）
- 2回のリクエストの間に改版が入っても版を取り違えない
- 著者を全文HTML側から取らずに済む（そちらは所属とメールアドレスが混ざる）

リンクが無い論文はアブストラクトだけを保存し、`fetch_complete` を false にします。

## 変換器を共有部品にした

ADR 0003でZenn用に書いたHTML→Markdown変換器を `src/html-markdown.ts` へ切り出しました。従来はZenn固有の分岐が共有部分の `switch` に直接書かれており、arXiv固有の分岐をそこへ足すと1つの部品に2サイトぶんの固有ルールが並ぶ形になります。2つ目の利用者が現れて境界が見えたので、ここで分けました。

- 共有部品からサイト名が消え、固有の要素はルール（インライン用・ブロック用の関数1つずつ）として外から渡す
- 相対URLの解決は共有部品側へ移動。HTMLの相対URLを文書のURLで解決するのは一般的な意味であり、サイト固有の話ではない
- 依存パッケージは追加していない

**等価であることは、既存のZennのテストを1行も変えずに通すことで確認しています。**

arXiv固有として足したのは3つだけです。数式（LaTeX原文が属性にあり、共通処理へ落とすとMathMLとTeX注釈が二重に出る）、アルゴリズムの擬似コード（`<pre>` ではなく行ごとの `div` で、放置すると1行ずつ段落へ割れる）、タイトルと抄録の間の書誌の飾り（著者の連絡先1,500字とCCS分類。落とさないとダイジェストの抜粋が抄録へ届かない）。

図には固有ルールを置いていません。相対URLさえ解決すれば共通処理が `![alt](url)` を出します。

## canonical

`https://arxiv.org/abs/{id}`（版なし）に寄せます。absページの `link rel="canonical"` が版を落としたURLを指しており、arXiv自身がバージョンを別資源ではなく同一資源の版として扱っているためです。`/abs/` `/html/` `/pdf/`、`www.` 付き、旧ID形式（`hep-th/9108001`）がすべて同じ1件になります。

版は落とすので、取得した版はフロントマターの `source_version` に残します。

判断の根拠と代替案は [ADR 0024](docs/adr/0024-arxiv-full-text-from-latexml-html.md) にあります。

## 確認したこと

- `pnpm test`（169件）・`pnpm typecheck`・`pnpm dry-run`
- 実際のarXivへリクエストを投げて、Workerと同じランタイムで端から端まで。`/pdf/` のURLから canonical・版 `v2`・著者11名・数式106+5・図2枚（相対URLの残りゼロ）・サイドバーとメールアドレスの混入ゼロ

## 確認していないこと

- **Slackから投げる往復は試していません。** 取得と変換は実物を通していますが、Slack→Queue→GitHub保存の経路は動かしていません。この経路で変わったのは `source_version` が1行増えることだけで、そこは単体テストで押さえています。
- **全文HTMLが無い論文のフォールバックを、実在の論文で試せていません。** 2007年から2026年まで8本当たって全部にHTML版があり、反例が見つかりませんでした。合成データの単体テストのみです。

author: boesee
body:
## Summary

You asked about matchup/opponent data missing since the rebuild. Checked the full FantasyPros OpenAPI spec you provided: zero matches for "matchup", "opponent", or "star_rating" anywhere - the proprietary matchup-favorability rating from the old scraped product isn't available via their public API at all, only on the website itself. Per our discussion, that rating is dropped entirely (not worth reintroducing scraping for), but the plain opponent is addable via ESPN's public scoreboard API, which you confirmed works and gave real data for.

### What this adds

`fetchOpponents(season, week)` in `scripts/update-rankings.mjs`:

```
GET https://site.api.espn.com/apis/site/v2/sports/football/nfl/scoreboard?week={week}&seasontype=2&year={season}
```

- Builds a `team_id -> "vs XXX"/"at XXX"` map from the week's games.
- Translates the two team abbreviations that differ from FantasyPros' (confirmed against your real responses): ESPN `JAX` → FantasyPros `JAC`, ESPN `WSH` → FantasyPros `WAS`.
- A fetch failure logs and continues with an empty map (`opponent: null` for everyone) rather than failing the whole run - unlike the rankings themselves, opponent isn't critical enough to block a commit over.

Documented in `architecture.md` (new "Gegner-Anreicherung" section, including why the matchup rating was dropped) and `entity_model.md`.

## Test plan

- [x] `node --check scripts/update-rankings.mjs`
- [x] Verified the team-abbreviation translation against your real SEA/NE and WSH/PHI/JAX examples
- [x] Full pipeline run with both APIs mocked: SEA correctly gets `"vs NE"`, NE gets `"at SEA"`
- [ ] Re-run `update-rankings.yml` and confirm `data/rankings.json` now has `opponent` populated

author: benbellot26
body:
## Summary

Hardens Pulsar V14 certification, market provenance, close capture, execution accounting and production safeguards without changing the champion probability engine.

### Invariants
- Software version -> `14.5.2`
- `MODEL_GENERATION` remains `pulsar-v14-context-v3`
- No champion probability-source file changed
- No staking policy changed
- No challenger or shadow module is promoted

### Certification hardening
- Requires freshness of underlying settled observations, not only report `generated_at`
- Versions the active probability/calibration policy independently with `PROBABILITY_POLICY_ID`
- Calibration evidence now requires exact current policy and generation
- Betting certification uses executable entry implied probability vs verified <=15m no-vig sharp fair close as primary CLV
- Requires independent same-book execution CLV evidence as a secondary gate
- Requires recent market-specific certified close observations

### Market / execution hardening
- Exchange-only sharp consensus remains research evidence but cannot authorize a real `BET`
- Decision and production runtime independently require at least one validated sharp sportsbook contributor
- ML/RL close capture no longer depends on a Total line being available
- Production acquisition now checks matched Odds games / scheduled MLB games in addition to priced / matched coverage
- Uncertainty artifacts require exact `MODEL_GENERATION`

### Ledger semantics
- Existing automatic bet ledger is explicitly `SYSTEM_AUTHORIZED_BET`, not proof of user execution
- Adds a separate explicit `REAL_EXECUTION` ledger that cannot be populated automatically by the prediction runtime
- Preserves compatibility with legacy authorized-ledger rows

### Governance
- Adds a generation-bound champion source manifest; CI fails if probability-bearing champion sources mutate without explicit review
- Adds production-workflow regression guard CI for production, close-capture, performance and reference-data workflow changes
- Expands regression tests for stale evidence, executable CLV, exchange-only sharp, slate coverage, close independence and authorized-vs-executed ledger boundaries

This PR intentionally does **not** fabricate or promote statistical evidence. Current betting certification must still be earned prospectively under the hardened contracts.

author: rmabon
body:
## Summary

Claude Code changed the Agent tool's contract: the `run_in_background` input parameter is gone — every subagent now launches async, and the launch is signalled only in the PostToolUse payload's `tool_response`:

```json
"tool_response": {
  "isAsync": true,
  "status": "async_launched",
  "agentId": "a96878d323c3010fc",
  ...
}
```

(Shape captured from a live hook by instrumenting a provisioned `write-state.sh` and launching a throwaway subagent.)

The `add-subagent` handler gated marker creation on `"run_in_background": true`, so new-format launches never wrote a `subagent__<id>` marker and the overview never showed `B` for a running background subagent.

**Fix:** add an `is_async_launch` check (`"isAsync": true` in the payload) and accept it alongside the legacy input flag. Old background payloads also carried `isAsync: true`, so it's the stable signal across both formats; legacy clients keep working unchanged. The reap paths (`clear-completed` / `reconcile`) were never broken — the completion `<task-id>` and Stop's `background_tasks` still carry the same `agentId` the marker is keyed on — they just never had a marker to reap.

Rollout note: the fix reaches a worktree's provisioned copy on its next `agent-new` after reinstalling the tool (provisioning rewrites the script unconditionally).

## Test plan

- New `test_add_subagent_new_format_without_run_in_background`, with a fixture modeled byte-for-byte on the captured live payload — written first and confirmed failing before the fix.
- `make check` — ruff clean, 849 passed.
- Live end-to-end in a dogfooded worktree: deployed the fixed script, launched a background subagent, `pending-<pane>/subagent__<id>` appeared at launch and was reaped after Stop.

author: shichuanliujie9527
body:
## Motivation

Two common test base classes hard-code backend selection, so accelerators outside the hard-coded lists resolve the wrong backend:

- `ShardedTensorTestBase.with_comms` / `init_pg` default to `"nccl"`: on other accelerators every bare `@with_comms` test is skipped, and migrated test files each carry a module-level `backend` global passed explicitly — review feedback on #192321 asks for this to come from the base class, which does not expose backend resolution today.
- `init_pg` gates backends behind a hard-coded allowlist and only binds the accelerator device for nccl/xccl (`hccl` passes the allowlist but never gets a device bound).
- `DistributedTestBase.backend` maps cuda/hpu/xpu explicitly and everything else to `"gloo"`, and `create_pg` probes `torch.accelerator.current_accelerator()` to pick the device to bind even though the device is passed in.

## Change

`ShardedTensorTestBase` (`distributed/_shard/sharded_tensor/__init__.py`):
- add a `backend` property resolving the default backend from the `device_type` injected by `instantiate_device_type_tests`; classes not instantiated per device type, and devices without a registered default backend, keep the historical `"nccl"` backend selection
- `with_comms` / `init_comms` / `init_pg` default `backend=None` and resolve through that property; explicit backend values are still passed through unchanged
- `init_pg`: drop the hard-coded allowlist (`init_process_group` validates backends itself) and bind the device for any non-gloo backend
- `with_comms` skip check: replace the hard-coded `["nccl", "xccl", "hccl"]` list with `!= "gloo"` and use `torch.accelerator.device_count()` directly; this removes the `current_accelerator()` probe, backend-to-device reverse lookup, and defensive `device_type is None` branches

`DistributedTestBase` (`common_distributed.py`):
- `backend(device)` resolves via `get_default_backend_for_device` instead of the hard-coded chain; devices without a registered default backend keep the old `gloo` fallback (the previous `else` branch). PrivateUse1 needs no special-casing here: `get_default_backend_for_device` normalizes the device string via `torch.device(...)`, which already maps privateuse1 to the registered backend name
- `create_pg` binds the device from the injected `device` argument for any non-gloo backend instead of probing `current_accelerator()`

## Behavior

| call site | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `with_comms(backend=...)` explicit | as passed | backend value unchanged (only `None` resolves) |
| bare `@with_comms`, class instantiated per device type | nccl: runs on CUDA, skips elsewhere | backend resolved from the injected `device_type`, runs |
| bare `@with_comms`, class not instantiated per device type | nccl default | backend selection remains nccl |
| `init_pg` backend validation | 5-name allowlist | `init_process_group` validates |
| `init_pg` / `create_pg` device binding | nccl/xccl only (hccl never bound) | any non-gloo backend |
| `with_comms` skip check | accelerator/backend matching plus device count | non-gloo backend plus `torch.accelerator.device_count()` |
| `DistributedTestBase.backend`, cuda/xpu/hpu/cpu | nccl/xccl/hccl/gloo | unchanged (same values via the map) |
| `DistributedTestBase.backend`, other accelerators | gloo (wrong) | registered default backend |

Follow-up (separate PRs): migrated test files can then drop their module-level `backend` globals and use bare `@with_comms`.

Same resolution shape as the `MultiProcContinuousTest`-side rework in #194152; this PR covers the two `MultiProcessTestCase`-side base classes only. #190528 touches the same `with_comms`/`init_pg` region — whichever lands second rebases.

## Test plan

- 4-accelerator host: `test_checkpoint.py` covers the explicit-backend path; bare `@with_comms` and `DistributedTestBase` suites resolve the device default and run.
- CUDA / CPU hosts: covered by CI.

author: osdiab
body: ## What does this PR do? Fix a High-severity admin magic-link auth bypass in `useVerificationToken` (`lib/nextAuthAdapter.ts`). NextAuth's email callback treats a non-null adapter result as a valid invite and does **not** re-compare the submitted token. This adapter looked up by identifier (email) only, compared tokens only to decide whether to delete, then still returned the stored row on mismatch. If SMTP + `NEXTAUTH_ACL` were enabled and any unused magic link existed for an ACL email, an incorrect `token` query param still authenticated. Changes: - Return `null` on token mismatch (do not return the stored token) - Compare with `crypto.timingSafeEqual` on equal-length buffers - Delete the stored token only after a successful match - Add unit tests for wrong / correct / reused token paths Branch is based on `ory/polis` `main` (not fork-only Cloud Agent commits) so the same patch can be proposed upstream later. Closes BRZ-2318 ## Type of change - [x] Bug fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue) ## How should this be tested? - [x] Existing unit tests - [x] New unit tests in `npm/test/next-auth/nextAuthAdapter.test.ts` (wrong token fails and keeps outstanding token; correct token succeeds once; reuse fails) - Manual / HTTP: outstanding magic link + wrong `token` → `/api/auth/error?error=Verification`; correct token → `/admin` with session cookie ## Checklist: - [x] My code follows the style guidelines of this project - [x] I have performed a self-review of my own code and corrected any misspellings - [ ] I have commented my code, particularly in hard-to-understand areas - [ ] I have made corresponding changes to the documentation - [x] My changes generate no new warnings - [x] I have added tests that prove my fix is effective or that my feature works - [x] New and existing unit tests pass locally with my changes

author: alexandre-schaffner
body:
The "Review new commits" action on the superseded-walkthrough toast called `handleRegenerate()` directly, so the incremental walkthrough ran against the stale diff still loaded in the page — the toast and the tab-side Pull button did different things. It now routes through `reviewLatestCommit()`, which pulls the new head first and only starts the incremental regeneration once the fresh diff is installed.

To make that sequencing possible, `pullLatestCommit()` returns a `Promise<boolean>` and coalesces concurrent callers on a shared in-flight promise, so a second caller awaits the same pull instead of returning early with no signal about the outcome. The ordering rule itself lives in `$lib/review/review-new-commits.ts` with unit tests covering both the happy path and the pull-failed case.

Also adds an unrelated dev-tooling commit: a `prepare` script that clones `Effect-TS/effect-smol` into a gitignored `.repos/effect` for local reference. Note this runs on every `bun install`, including CI — happy to drop that commit if it wasn't meant for this PR.

body:
## Problem Backend CI keeps a draft PR waiting about a minute at the end of a run that executed no tests at all. A draft whose test selection cannot be trusted skips both the Django and the product matrices and defers to the ready-for-review run. Two reporting jobs do not know that and run anyway. - `report-test-timings` downloads no JUnit and emits no traces. It sits after the `Django Tests Pass` gate, so its whole duration lands on the wall. - `test-selection-verdict` regenerates a selection and scores it against JUnit that does not exist. That costs about two minutes of runner time. [This run](https://github.com/PostHog/posthog/actions/runs/33008467049) is the shape: 5m45 wall, and the traces job is the last minute of it. ## Changes - Backend CI now ends about a minute earlier on a draft that ran no tests. - `report-test-timings` and `test-selection-verdict` skip when both matrices were skipped. - The selection decision is still recorded. `capture-test-selection` reports the mode and the skip reason, and already gates on an empty mode. - Mechanical: `django` and `turbo-tests` join the `needs` of `report-test-timings` for their results. `django_tests` already waits for both, so this adds no wall time. - Mechanical: the Depot shadow strips both jobs, so only its header note changes. Nothing in the product looks different. This changes CI wiring only. Before, on a draft that ran no tests: ```mermaid flowchart LR D[Django matrix
skipped] --> G{{Django Tests Pass}} P[Product matrix
skipped] --> G D --> V[Test selection verdict
runs] P --> V G --> T[Report per-test traces
runs] T --> E[Run ends] classDef phBlue fill:#1d4aff,stroke:#1d4aff,color:#fff; classDef phRed fill:#f54e00,stroke:#f54e00,color:#fff; classDef phYellow fill:#f9bd2b,stroke:#f9bd2b,color:#000; classDef phGray fill:#e5e7eb,stroke:#c7ccd1,color:#000; class D,P phGray; class G phBlue; class V,T phRed; class E phYellow; ``` After: ```mermaid flowchart LR D[Django matrix
skipped] --> G{{Django Tests Pass}} P[Product matrix
skipped] --> G D --> V[Test selection verdict
skipped] P --> V G --> T[Report per-test traces
skipped] G --> E[Run ends] classDef phBlue fill:#1d4aff,stroke:#1d4aff,color:#fff; classDef phYellow fill:#f9bd2b,stroke:#f9bd2b,color:#000; classDef phGray fill:#e5e7eb,stroke:#c7ccd1,color:#000; class D,P,V,T phGray; class G phBlue; class E phYellow; ``` ## How did you test this code? No test covers a workflow condition, so this PR is its own two-stage check. - As a draft, both matrices skip, so both reporting jobs must show as skipped and the run must end at the gate. - Marking it ready runs the matrices, so both jobs must run and report as they do today. Local linters pass, including the Depot shadow-drift check. `actionlint` reports no finding that master does not already report. Not run: nothing here can be exercised outside GitHub Actions. ## Automatic notifications - [ ] Publish to changelog? ## Docs update None. ## 🤖 Agent context **Autonomy:** Human-driven (agent-assisted) Written by Claude Code. Skills invoked: `/authoring-ci-workflows`, `/writing-pr-descriptions`, `/reviewing-before-pr`, `/babysit-pr`. The session started from a wider list of waste in draft runs and dropped two candidates after checking the repo. Caching the OpenAPI gate fails because generation is not a pure function of the source tree: it is not idempotent across environments, and an enum added in one product renames another product's generated enum, so the key would cover the whole tree and miss on every backend PR. Gating the migration replay on the `migrations` paths filter fails because `uv.lock` is already part of the migration set, since a dependency bump can carry third-party migrations. author: delphinus
body:
Make cutting a release just pushing a tag, and let the release notes be written in the repository
beforehand.

## Why

`bin/set-tag` tagged, downloaded the tarball, rewrote the formula, committed and pushed, all from
the local machine, and the GitHub Release itself was made by hand afterwards. It is easy to get
halfway through and hard to retry.

## How it works now

1. Write the release notes in `.github/release-notes/vX.Y.Z.md`. The first line is the title of
   the release, and the rest is its body.
2. Merge them into `master`.
3. Run `bin/release X.Y.Z`.

`bin/release` does nothing but check and tag. It refuses to run unless

* the version is a semver,
* the notes for it exist,
* the current branch is `master`, the working tree is clean and it is the same as `origin/master`,
* the tag does not exist yet, and
* the build check of `HEAD` is green (`FORCE=1` skips this one).

Then `.github/workflows/release.yml` (`on: push: tags: v*`) runs `bin/github-release.sh`, which

* refuses to go on if the tag is not on `master`,
* creates the release with the notes (or with `--generate-notes` if they are missing),
* rewrites `url` / `version` / `sha256` of the formula with the sha256 of the tarball of the tag,
  and commits it into `master` as `Update formula to use new version`.

Both steps are idempotent: an existing release and an up-to-date formula are left alone, so the
job can be re-run when a half of it fails.

## Notes

* The formula is pushed with `SSH_PRIVATE_KEY`, as `bin/github-generate-doc.sh` already does.
  `master` is a protected branch and pushing with `GITHUB_TOKEN` is rejected.

author: jungley8
body:
💡 **What:** 
The optimization addresses the N+1 database query issue in `emailBounceWebhook`. Specifically, we transitioned from fetching `Mailbox` records and writing `AuditLog`/`MailSuppression` records sequentially in a loop to querying/inserting them in batch operations (e.g. `IN (?)` queries and bulk inserts). Notification dispatching was also updated to capture variable arguments securely in goroutines to prevent variable capture bugs, and to respect concurrency.

🎯 **Why:** 
Processing mass bounce webhooks involved looping over events and sequentially querying the database to find `Mailbox`es, insert `AuditLog`s, update `MailSuppression`s via `OnConflict`, and retrieve `NotificationChannel`s. This approach scales poorly. Using bulk queries/updates drastically reduces database round-trips (I/O) and CPU overhead per webhook request.

📊 **Measured Improvement:** 
Created a new benchmark `BenchmarkEmailBounceWebhook` simulating 100 bounce events payload in `plugins/mail/bounce_benchmark_test.go`.
- **Baseline:** ~34.1ms per operation
- **Optimized:** ~11.3ms per operation
- **Improvement:** ~67% reduction in processing time (or roughly a 3x speedup).

body:
Ten open bug reports against v0.28.0 and a wider announcement due next week — the README should not read as settled software. It did.

## The notice

States the stage as a fact and backs it with real numbers rather than a hedge: **32 releases since 22 July, fourteen of them on a single day, one yanked.** That pace is the honest evidence in both directions — it's why bugs exist *and* why they get fixed the same day.

Three expectations set explicitly:

- **Known bugs in the current release**, with the issue tracker named as the live and authoritative list. Deliberately **a link, not an enumeration** — the README shipped to PyPI is frozen at each release, so a list of specific bugs would be wrong the moment they were fixed. The file says that about itself.
- **Breaking changes before 1.0.0**, pointing at `API-STABILITY.md` — which already said *"pre-1.0.0 nothing is frozen"*. The README just never repeated it where a reader would see it.
- **Docs that can lag the code**, with today's two corrections named, and the rule stated: **if code and prose disagree, the code is right** — and please report it.

Then practical advice, none of it hypothetical: destructive capabilities are off until an operator names them and the allowlists fail closed; `apply_comment_actions` defaults to a dry run and should be read before applying, because it posts under your name to a document colleagues are reading; try the write path somewhere you can afford to break it; and `report_a_problem` assembles the diagnostic for you.

It still closes on what's solid, because underselling is its own inaccuracy: feature-complete for the scoped roadmap, live-verified against real Google, **963 offline tests**, ruff and mypy clean across 3.10–3.14.

## Also fixes a stale claim in the first screenful — live on PyPI now

> *"Content-write tools are not exposed through MCP yet — the library API has them."*

Content writes shipped through MCP in **v0.13.0**, fifteen releases ago; Docs suggestions in v0.20.0. Same defect family as the dangling `library only` reference fixed in #160 this morning, and about the worst possible placement — the first thing a PyPI visitor reads.

Now says the server reaches everything the library does, with the tool count (**34**) verified against the registry rather than counted by hand.

## Tests

963 passed. `test_readme_tools.py` still agrees with the tool registry.

Every anchor in the new block verified to resolve — my first draft pointed at `#configuration`, which doesn't exist, inside the same paragraph promising the docs can be trusted. Fixed to `#capability-boundaries`.

author: soulmamascateringmudgee-cell
body:
Mudgee has no wholesaler for half a catering list, so the same job gets shopped across Woolworths, Coles and Aldi. The price list could not describe that — one row per ingredient meant recording the Coles price **silently erased the Aldi one**, and the question a caterer actually asks ("which of the three should I drive to") had nowhere to live.

## What changes

**An ingredient now holds a price per shop**, and costing takes the cheapest it can honestly compare, naming the shop on the line. A total that doesn't tell you where to go is not a shopping plan.

The job also reports what shopping around saved against buying the lot at the dearest shop.

```
Beef brisket    $32.00   2 kg × $16.00 at Aldi
                $44.00 elsewhere
```

**Cheapest never means comparing units that don't line up.** $2 a bunch is not cheaper than $8 a kilo — it's a different way of buying parsley. A price whose unit can't be reconciled with the order line is dropped from the comparison rather than allowed to win it. An item priced *only* in an unusable unit is still reported as a mismatch, exactly as before.

**Receipts get their own reader.** A supermarket receipt is not a wholesale docket, and reading it as one gets the quantities wrong: a docket has a quantity column, a Woolworths receipt mostly hides the amount inside the product name (`MILK FC 2L`) — precisely the noise the wholesale prompt is told to strip out. Loose produce is the reverse, printing its own weight and per-kilo rate on a second line. Add discount lines, and a GST summary that means something different when most of a caterer's basket is GST-free fresh food. So there are two modes and the reader is told which it's looking at, rather than one prompt with caveats.

**The review comparison is keyed by item *and* shop.** Comparing an Aldi receipt line against the Woolworths price on file would have reported a 30% fall that was really just two different shops — the confident wrong number this app exists to avoid.

## Schema (migration 0007)

`supplier` becomes `NOT NULL DEFAULT ''`, and the unique key becomes `(user_id, item, supplier)`.

Nullable would let unlimited shopless duplicates back in, since NULLs are distinct from each other in a Postgres unique constraint — the same silent-overwrite bug wearing a different hat. A unique index over `coalesce(supplier,'')` fixes that but **cannot be named as a conflict target through PostgREST**, which only accepts plain column lists, so every upsert would have become a read-then-write race.

A `BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE` trigger coalesces an explicit NULL to `''`. A migration and a deploy cannot land in the same instant, and without it that gap is a window where saving any price fails outright.

## Checks

- 152 tests pass (7 new on shop pricing: cheapest wins, the shop is named, savings reported, one shop claims no saving, incomparable units are excluded not compared, unusable-unit-only is still a mismatch, and convertible units across shops still compare)
- `tsc --noEmit` clean, `next build` clean
- **Verified against the live database**, not just asserted: three shops coexist on one ingredient; re-recording one shop's price updates that shop and leaves the others alone; an explicit NULL supplier lands as `''`. Test rows removed afterwards — the table is back to empty.

## Note on what this isn't

This doesn't scrape Woolworths or Coles. Their terms prohibit it, both run bot protection, and a weekly scraper would be a thing that breaks quietly and then feeds stale prices into quotes. Photographing the receipt gets what was *actually paid* — including Aldi, which publishes almost nothing online.

author: messold-technologies
body:
> **Stacked on [#230](https://github.com/Messold-Technologies1/UGC-PLATFORM/pull/230)** — both touch `instagram-media.service.ts` and `use-instagram-reels.ts`. Its diff disappears from here once #230 merges. Review the second commit (`da935af`).

## The waste

The picker polled `instagram/media/status` every **2.5s** for as long as the server said "syncing". But the queue deliberately holds a sync much longer than that:

| Backpressure state | Hold | Requests burned at 2.5s |
|---|---|---|
| `SLOW_MS` (usage ≥75%) | 60s | 24 |
| `PAUSE_MS` (usage ≥90%) | 10 min | 240 |
| `BREAKER_PAUSE_MS` (5 rate limits) | 15 min | **360** |

The breaker opens precisely when a lot of creators are importing at once — so the load spike and the polling spike coincide. Each request is a Postgres read of `instagramMediaSyncState` answering "still working".

Worse: the route is throttled at **120/min** and one tab polls at **24/min**, so **five tabs trip the creator's own throttle** and the gallery starts erroring while nothing is actually wrong.

## The fix

The queue already knows when a batch finishes, and #228 put the transport in place. `syncConnectionMedia` now emits `instagram.reel_sync_updated` to the creator's `user:` room and any admin in the `portfolio:<id>` room; `RealtimeProvider` invalidates the reel query prefix, which covers the gallery pages and the status read for both the creator's own view and an admin's.

Emitted on **all three** outcomes, not just success:

- **success** — with `reelCount` and `hasMore`
- **failure** — otherwise the spinner sits there until the backstop notices
- **no-op extend** — "Load more" on a fully cached account spends no Graph call at all, but the reader is already looking at a spinner that only an event takes down

One subtlety in the payload: a `refresh` walks the top of the account and deliberately leaves the paging frontier alone, so it reports the *stored* `hasMore` rather than its own local view — otherwise it would tell the client the account had been exhausted.

## Not zero polling, deliberately

A lost event here strands a **spinner**, which is a worse failure than the mirror's stale badge in #228. So the status read stays — at **90s instead of 2.5s**:

- ~10 requests across a breaker pause instead of 360 (**36× cut**)
- still able to distinguish "still queued" from "we missed the event", which matters because a 10–15 minute hold is legitimate and no event is coming yet

Plus the reconnect reconcile from #228, extended to the reel keys. The socket is what actually ends the wait; the interval only exists so the UI cannot hang.

## Queued vs fetching

`SyncStatus` already distinguished `QUEUED` from `SYNCING` and the picker collapsed both into one spinner. A bare spinner through a 10-minute queue hold reads as broken, so a queued sync now says *"You're in the queue — we'll start fetching your reels in a moment"* / *"Waiting for Instagram — this can take a few minutes when a lot of creators are importing at once."* No new data; it was already in the payload.

## Wiring

`SocialConnectionsModule` now imports `RealtimeModule`. No cycle — `RealtimeModule` pulls only Prisma and Jwt.

## Verification

- server `jest`: **323 passing** / 36 suites, up from 316, same 3 pre-existing suite failures as `development`
- server `tsc`: holds at its 2 pre-existing errors
- client `tsc` and `eslint` clean

New coverage: the sync announcing a finished batch with its count, announcing a **failure**, announcing a **no-op extend** without spending a Graph call, and reporting the stored frontier after a refresh rather than the batch's local view; plus the notifier reaching both rooms, normalising optional fields to `null` so the client can tell "not reported" from a real zero, and swallowing a notification failure rather than failing the sync that succeeded.

Not verified in a browser.
